AI for skin cancer: the ISIC community

Background report for the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) meeting handout. Prepared 21 September 2026.

553,019public images in the ISIC Archive
1,207,517images in total
62collections, about 22 with DOIs
45researchers profiled
278shared AI and imaging papers, 2023–2026

For the past decade, the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) has driven dermatology AI research by curating open benchmark datasets and running competitive image-classification challenges. Recent challenges have shifted toward releasing winning model weights and code directly to the community, giving machine learning teams reproducible state-of-the-art baselines and providing clinical investigators inspectable tools for validation studies.

Three recent milestones highlight this shift. First, the SLICE-3D dataset and the ISIC 2024 challenge established 3D total-body photography (3D-TBP) as an open benchmark, showing that incorporating patient-level spatial context improves lesion triage over single-lesion classification [1, 2]. Second, PanDerm demonstrated the utility of a shared dermatology foundation model evaluated across four distinct imaging modalities in clinician-in-the-loop studies [3]. Third, investigators published the first randomized controlled trial evaluating 3D-TBP in clinical practice alongside an empirical cost-effectiveness analysis [4, 5].

Recent community studies also outline where current systems fail. They include "AI in skin cancer diagnosis: a reality check" (2024) [6], "Limits of AI models for skin cancer diagnosis in realistic settings" (2026) [7], a calibration audit of the leading ISIC 2020 models [8], and two 2026 studies showing that a validated early-detection toolkit improved accuracy without reducing the number of biopsies [9, 10]. Further progress will require shifting metrics from narrow diagnostic classification toward actionable management recommendations, integrating multimodal patient data, and ensuring calibrated performance across varied skin types and acquisition hardware. While the ISIC Archive now hosts the patient-level, longitudinal, and multimodal records needed to tackle these challenges, these capabilities remain underused across the research community.

The ISIC Archive underpins this work. It now holds 553,019 public images (1.2 million in total) in 62 collections [11], about 22 of which carry citable DataCite DOIs. Its infrastructure is funded mainly by two NIH/NCI U24 grants to Memorial Sloan Kettering (MSKCC) and Shore Family philanthropic funding. The science around it is supported by EU projects (iToBoS, MELCAYA), Australian programs (the ACRF-funded ACEMID network and NHMRC grants), the Melanoma Research Alliance and the US Department of Defense.

To see who does this work, we cross-indexed the full 2023–2026 publication lists of 45 researchers: Organizing Committee members, AI Working Group members, the leads of the other working groups, and six other groups connected to ISIC. This produced 278 multi-author papers on AI, imaging and digital health. The resulting collaboration network has four hubs of roughly equal weight: Queensland (Soyer), Barcelona (Malvehy and Puig), Vienna (Kittler and Tschandl) and MSKCC (Halpern and Rotemberg). MSKCC is central through the Archive and the challenges; the other three are bound more tightly to each other through joint clinical studies. Several active groups sit outside this core, including those working on robustness, data quality, image acquisition and data standards, and they are the most promising places to start new collaborations.

This report outlines recent research milestones across the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC), details active research priorities among consortium investigators, and directs readers to the appropriate leads for prospective partnerships. By highlighting underused archive capabilities, including longitudinal tracking, multimodal image pairing, and content-based image retrieval, we invite external groups to contribute datasets and join active studies supporting standardized, early skin cancer detection.

SLICE-3D and ISIC 2024

400,000 lesion crops from 3D total-body scans became an open benchmark. The winning triage model reached an AUC of 0.967, and patient context measurably helped.

PanDerm

The first dermatology foundation model evaluated with clinicians across four imaging modalities, pretrained on 2.1 million images from 11 institutions.

From 2D dermoscopy to the whole patient: 3D total-body photography

3D total-body photography (3D-TBP) is the line of work that has gone furthest in this period, from dataset to trial. The ISIC AI Working Group initiated SLICE-3D (Kurtansky et al.) [1], a dataset of 400,000 lesion crops extracted from Canfield Vectra WB360 scans contributed by seven institutions: MSKCC, Hospital Clínic Barcelona, Queensland, Vienna, Athens, Melanoma Institute Australia and University Hospital Basel. It formed the basis of the ISIC 2024 Kaggle challenge, which drew 2,739 teams [2, 12]. The follow-up analysis (Kurtansky et al., with Rotemberg and Kose as joint senior authors) [2] reported that the winning model reached an AUC of 0.967 and, at 80% sensitivity, flagged roughly one cancer per 52 triaged lesions, against one per 1,100 at baseline. The study showed that patient context (the "ugly duckling" sign) was effective in the winning model.

In parallel, ISIC's Australian partners supplied the clinical evidence. Soyer and colleagues published the first randomized clinical trial of 3D-TBP in high-risk patients [4], together with a cost-effectiveness analysis in the same issue [5]. Queensland then used 3D-TBP data to identify phenotypes associated with late-onset melanoma [13], to classify photodamage automatically (with Ge's group at Monash) [14], to measure skin color objectively [15], and even to estimate body mass index and screen for obesity-related comorbidity [16, 17]. The iToBoS consortium, coordinated from the University of Girona, published its own 3D-TBP dataset (Saha et al.: 16,954 images from 100 participants in Barcelona and Brisbane) [18] and an annotation protocol led by Clare Primiero [19]. Barcelona has since tested an autonomous total-body and dermoscopy device against standard dermatoscopes [20], and Girona is building a multi-robot full-body scanner [21]. At MSKCC, the first clinical assessment of the ISIC 2024 triage algorithm on real 3D-TBP data is underway [22].

Foundation models and vision-language models

PanDerm (Yan et al.) [3] was built at Monash by Zongyuan Ge's group with Kittler, Tschandl, Soyer and Guitera. It was pretrained on 2.1 million images from 11 institutions across dermoscopy, clinical photographs, 3D-TBP and dermatopathology. In clinical evaluations it outperformed clinicians in early melanoma detection from longitudinal images, improved dermatologists' accuracy on dermoscopy by 11%, and improved non-specialists' differential diagnosis by 16.5% across 128 conditions. Its successor, a zero-shot vision-language model with automated concept discovery, followed in 2026 [23]. The same group released Derm1M, a million-pair image–text dataset [24], and has moved on to agentic and reasoning systems such as DermAgent and DermoGPT [25, 26].

At Stanford, Daneshjou's group built MONET, an image–text model grounded in the dermatology literature [27], whose concept scores are now distributed with the MILK10k dataset [28]. MSKCC and Northeastern University fine-tuned a general multimodal large language model (Qwen 2 VL) to predict 16 quantitative lesion attributes, such as lesion area, border irregularity and color contrast, from SLICE-3D images (Torop et al., with Kose as senior author) [29]. The model predicted these attributes with R² between 0.71 and 0.96, and its internal representations proved useful for content-based image retrieval: they return images that look like a query image and can be tuned to also match it on a chosen attribute, outperforming the untuned model and MONET's image encoder on attribute-matched retrieval. This model now powers the content-based image retrieval capability of the ISIC Archive (Section 4).

Codella's group at Microsoft works on the general-purpose alternative. Their open medical embedding model (MedImageInsight) [30] and their Nature Medicine 2026 stress test of frontier models ("the illusion of readiness") [31] raise a question the talk is likely to be asked: do dermatology-specific foundation models still beat general ones?

Human–AI collaboration and explainability

The community's most-cited result on human–AI interaction remains Barata and colleagues' reinforcement-learning model (with Rotemberg, Tschandl, Kittler and others) [32]. By encoding clinician and patient preferences as rewards, it raised melanoma sensitivity from 61.4% to 79.5% and improved dermatologists' correct diagnoses by 12%. This is significant because it targets the management decision, not the label.

Explainability is now being tested on people rather than asserted. Within 18 months, three independent studies measured it with eye tracking or reader experiments: MSKCC compared dermatologists' gaze with AI heat maps [33]; the Heidelberg group with Kittler showed that dermatologist-like explanations improve accuracy and trust [34, 35]; and a Nature Medicine 2026 study with Tschandl found that the same explanations help clinicians and lay users in different ways [36]. Kittler, Tschandl and Liopyris also led an international reader study showing that dermatoscopy-based models can predict melanoma metastasis [37].

Datasets, benchmarks and data quality

The period produced a new generation of curated datasets. MILK10k (Tschandl et al.) [28] pairs 10,480 dermoscopic and close-up images of 5,240 lesions from five centers, covers 48 ISIC-DX diagnoses, reports skin tone, and ships MONET concept scores; it was de-duplicated with the SelfClean method from Navarini's group in Basel [38]. MIDAS [39] links Stanford, MSKCC, Vienna and Seoul in one multimodal benchmark. Kittler's group added BALD for acral lesions [40]; Queensland added a longitudinal dataset of 3D-TBP tiles with matching dermoscopy (Ghahari et al.) [41]; Yap's group contributed ISIC-DICM-17K [42].

Data quality became a research topic in its own right, and users of the Archive have contributed to its quality assurance: Cassidy, Yap and Jaworek-Korjakowska identified duplicates and train–test leakage in earlier ISIC challenge sets [43]. Since then the Basel and Lucerne group has built a sequence of data-cleaning methods culminating in a NeurIPS 2024 audit technique [44] and the Cleanpatrick benchmark (with Tschandl) [45]. The community has also produced consensus diagnosis terminology (ISIC-DX) [46].

Fairness and skin tone

Work on equity has become more precise. MSKCC compared skin-tone scales prospectively for dataset labeling [47] and released a skin-tone labeling set with Fitzpatrick, Monk, Pantone and colorimeter readings [48]. Stanford extended its Diverse Dermatology Images collection [49] with DDI-2 for Asian patients [50] and documented skin-tone disparities in vision-language models [51]. Queensland now measures skin color directly from 3D-TBP [15]. MSKCC and Northeastern showed that the top ISIC 2020 models, despite high AUC, were poorly calibrated across various facets, such as sex, skin tone and age (Dominique et al.) [8], which argues for calibration by subgroup as a standard fairness metric.

Optical imaging beyond the dermatoscope

Reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) AI is an active line of work. Kose's group published a machine-learning model for non-invasive melanoma diagnosis with RCM (Kentley et al.) [52], extended RCM-AI to basal cell carcinoma depth [53] and to intra-operative margins in oral cancer [54], is deploying RCM in India with Tata Memorial [55], and has developed a generative method for synthesizing RCM views at new depths (CD-RCM) [56]. Stanford (Daneshjou and Zaba) [57] and Sydney (Guitera) [58] have published their own RCM deep-learning work. Recently, pilot RCM data have been uploaded to ISIC and can now be visualized with an integrated multimodal viewer. Beyond RCM, line-field confocal OCT (LC-OCT) is another imaging modality that has been increasingly studied in the field, including a multicenter study of AI-assisted basal cell carcinoma diagnosis [59], and Sydney is implementing LC-OCT clinically [60]. However, LC-OCT data have not yet been ingested into the ISIC Archive.

Large language models

General-purpose language and vision-language models are now being tested as diagnostic readers. Navarrete-Dechent's group compared ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude on basal cell carcinoma images [61] and ChatGPT-4 against CNNs on melanocytic lesions [62]. A Heidelberg study with Tschandl found that LLMs improve physician accuracy but encourage false reliance [63]. Daneshjou has moved largely into LLM evaluation and governance, including the MedHELM benchmark [64] and a NEJM AI argument for continuous post-clearance monitoring [65]. In Australia, Caffery and colleagues are informing a position statement on LLMs and AI scribes in dermatology [66].

Regulation, deployment and real-world performance

DermaSensor's De Novo authorization in January 2024 rested on the DERM-SUCCESS study (1,579 lesions in 22 primary-care sites), which reported 95.5% sensitivity and a 96.6% negative predictive value but only 20.7% specificity [67]. NICE's 2025 guidance allows DERM to be used in NHS teledermatology for three years while evidence is gathered, citing 97% sensitivity for cancer and 95% for melanoma in NHS data, and recommending dermatologist review for Fitzpatrick types V and VI [68]. The NHS 10-Year Health Plan states that AI-supported skin cancer pathways will be standard care by 2028 [69].

Prospective and real-world studies from ISIC groups temper these figures. MSKCC's PROVE-AI study reached 96.8% sensitivity and, with 37.4% specificity, saved one-third of benign biopsies [70]. Maul's group in Zürich documented inconsistent CNN outputs on repeated images in routine use [71]. Athens concluded that image-based AI is insufficient as a stand-alone assessment in real practice [72]. A 2026 JAMA Dermatology meta-analysis from the Heidelberg group now summarizes the prospective evidence for AI-assisted melanoma diagnosis [73].

Use of ISIC data across the field: a scoping review

We conducted a scoping review guided by JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR, searching five databases for original studies published from 2013 through August 2025 that used ISIC datasets for dermatologic AI research to understand the impact that the public ISIC Archive has had on the field. Of 5,194 records screened, 3,468 studies were included and verified as using ISIC datasets, which were used most often for training and internal validation, while external testing was substantially less common across the cohort. Model architectures evolved from classical machine learning to convolutional neural networks and, more recently, transformers and hybrid models. Authorship was concentrated in Asia, accounting for 65% of author-geography associations, whereas Europe and North America contributed the largest shares of ISIC datasets (figure below). This highlights how public datasets such as the ISIC Archive can have broad-ranging global impact. The review paper will soon be submitted for publication.

What the groups are working on now

Nine active themes and the groups driving each one.

Taken together, the publication record points to nine active themes. They are listed here with the groups that drive each one.

3D total-body photography and whole-patient triage

is the most mature, led by Queensland, MSKCC and Barcelona with Canfield Scientific as the common hardware partner [1, 4, 74]. The open problems are device independence and longitudinal change detection [2, 41, 75], and the only cost-effectiveness analysis so far is Australian [5].

Foundation, vision-language and agentic models

are led by Monash with Vienna and Queensland, by Stanford, and increasingly by industry [3, 24–27, 31]. The question has shifted from "can we build one" to "does it help clinicians, and does it generalize" [7].

Human–AI interaction and explainability tested on people/readers

is led by Vienna and Lisbon (reinforcement learning) [32], MSKCC (eye tracking) [33], Heidelberg with Vienna [34–36], and Zürich (self-supervised retrieval with reader studies) [76, 77].

What AI does not fix

is a theme in its own right. The Arizona–Oregon–Stanford group showed in two 2026 JID papers that a validated early-detection toolkit improved accuracy without improving the number needed to biopsy [9], and that much biopsy-decision variability is not predictable by AI [10]. Combined with the "reality check" and "limits" papers [6, 7], the calibration audit [8] and Rotemberg's 2026 editorial on AI screening and overdiagnosis [78], this literature argues that the management decision is the next target.

Data quality, curation and transparency

is led by Basel/Lucerne, Manchester, MSKCC and Vienna [28, 43–46].

Fairness and skin tone

is led by MSKCC, Stanford and Queensland, with measurement moving from Fitzpatrick self-report toward Monk scales, colorimetry and scanner-derived color [8, 15, 47, 50, 51].

New optical modalities

(RCM, LC-OCT, OCT angiography, multispectral and fluorescence imaging) are led by MSKCC, Stanford, Barcelona, Sydney, Vienna, Zürich, Arizona and Oregon [52, 57–60, 79–82]; pilot RCM data are now in the Archive, while LC-OCT data have not yet been ingested.

Large language models

as readers, scribes and patient-information sources are being evaluated at Stanford, Heidelberg, Santiago, MD Anderson and Queensland [61–64, 66, 83].

Robustness, security and standards

form a smaller but distinct cluster: adversarial attacks on ISIC-trained classifiers (Kraków) [84], domain adaptation (Manchester) [85], shortcut learning (Lisbon with Campinas) [86], out-of-distribution guardrails (Vitória, Brazil) [87, 88], and data standards beyond DICOM (DermIDS at Vanderbilt [89]; MedicalPhoto in Seoul [90]).

What the Archive holds

As of September 2026 the Archive's live counter [11] reports 553,019 public images and 1,207,517 in total, with more than 12,000 registered users, across 62 collections. It contains contact and polarized dermoscopy, clinical close-up and overview photographs, 3D-TBP tiles, segmentation masks and longitudinal series. Diagnoses follow the ISIC-DX consensus tree, and the anatomical-site taxonomy was updated in April 2026. Every image carries its own Creative Commons license (CC-0, CC-BY or CC-BY-NC). Data can be browsed in the gallery, searched by image through the Archive's content-based image retrieval (CBIR) capability, or downloaded through the API or the isic-cli command-line tool. The ISIC Archive is listed on the AWS Open Data registry, which adds long-term sustainability.

How the Archive is used

The Archive is the field's common benchmark and the training source for challenge entries. It is included in the pretraining corpus of foundation models such as PanDerm [3], and it is a test bed for fairness and data-quality audits. The NIH grant that funds it cites more than 2,500 citations and over 3,500 challenge participants. Users have provided extensive feedback on the Archive through their studies, helping with quality assurance by finding duplicates and leakage in the older challenge sets [43], shortcut artifacts such as rulers and ink, and under-representation of darker skin tones. The newer curated collections (ISIC Balanced, MILK10k, the novice segmentation masks) were created partly to address these.

How contributors obtain a DOI

  1. PrepareFormat images and metadata against the ISIC data dictionary, using the published metadata template.
  2. UploadUpload through the web interface or isic-cli and group the images into a collection.
  3. LicenseAssign a Creative Commons license (CC-0, CC-BY or CC-BY-NC) to each image.
  4. ReviewISIC staff review the submission for privacy and quality.
  5. MintISIC mints a DataCite DOI with the prefix 10.34970 against a frozen snapshot of the collection.

Standardized benchmarks are essential for evaluating dermatology models, and the ISIC Archive serves as the primary repository for this data. A contributing group prepares its images and metadata against the ISIC data dictionary using the published metadata template, uploads them through the web interface or isic-cli, and groups them into a collection. The contributor assigns a Creative Commons license to each image. ISIC staff review the submission for privacy and quality. ISIC then mints a DataCite DOI with the prefix 10.34970 against a frozen snapshot of the collection. The DOI landing page records the image count, description, supplementary files and related identifiers, such as the descriptor paper that describes the dataset. Users cite the collection DOI together with the per-image attributions.

About 22 collections currently carry DOIs, including SLICE-3D (the ISIC 2024 challenge data; 10.34970/2024-slice-3d), MILK10k (10.34970/648456), DERM12345 (10.34970/705541), iToBoS 2024 (10.34970/561126) and others.

What the Archive records that few people use

Fields in data dictionary v2.4 that support patient-level, longitudinal and multimodal work.

The vast majority of studies built on ISIC data use only the raw lesion crop and its primary diagnostic label. In contrast, the current ISIC Data Dictionary (version 2.4, April 2026), which builds on the structure introduced in version 2.0 (October 2024) [91], specifies granular patient-level, anatomical, and acquisition metadata. Paired with the archive's image-similarity search capabilities, this expanded schema provides the foundation for longitudinal lesion tracking, cross-modal analysis, and patient-contextual modeling, avenues of investigation that few research teams have pursued.

Provenance and licensing

Version 2.4 adds an image_manipulation field that separates unmodified instrument images from altered ones, such as images blurred to hide identifiers, and from synthetic images. As generated images enter public datasets, this field is the simplest safeguard against pretraining models on synthetic data or on editing artifacts. Licenses are recorded image by image in copyright_license (CC-0, CC-BY or CC-BY-NC), so training sets intended for commercial and academic use can be filtered programmatically rather than by collection.

Patient context and the "ugly duckling"

patient_id links all images of one person within an upload cohort. A model can therefore read a patient's other lesions and score each lesion against that person's own background, which is the computational form of the "ugly duckling" sign. The ISIC 2024 analysis showed that such patient-context features improve triage [2]; the field allows any collection that records it to support the same approach. personal_hx_mm and family_hx_mm record personal and first-degree family history of melanoma and can be used as priors in multimodal models. age_approx is binned to five-year intervals and capped at 85 to protect privacy while keeping the age structure needed for risk estimation.

Lesion timelines

lesion_id identifies one physical lesion across repeated imaging, and acquisition_day records when each image was taken, in days relative to the patient's other images (within a range of ±10,000 days). Together, these fields turn static images into sequences. They make it possible to train sequence models and spatio-temporal transformers that learn from change, reproducing what sequential digital dermoscopy imaging (SDDI) does clinically: detecting slowly evolving early melanomas that do not yet show classic dermoscopic criteria. The Queensland longitudinal tile dataset [41] and MSKCC's work on predicting malignancy in monitored lesions [92] show that such data exist; the dictionary gives them a common format. Patient and lesion identifiers are unique, so records can be linked across collections.

Multimodal and optical imaging

image_type has eight values: dermoscopic, two clinical views (overview and close-up), two 3D-TBP tile views, and three confocal types (RCM macroscopic, tile and mosaic). dermoscopic_type distinguishes contact polarized, contact non-polarized and non-contact polarized dermoscopy, and tbp_tile_type distinguishes 3D white-light, 3D cross-polarized and 2D tiles. Cross-polarized light removes surface glare and shows deeper pigment and vessels, so models can learn from both lightings of the same lesion. rcm_case_id groups the confocal images of one clinical session so they can be aligned. The schema therefore supports reflectance confocal microscopy: as noted in Section 1, pilot RCM data have recently been uploaded and can be viewed in the Archive's integrated multimodal viewer.

Histopathology and label quality

concomitant_biopsy marks images captured at or just before biopsy, so the image and the pathology report describe the same lesion at the same time; images taken weeks earlier may show a lesion that has since changed. diagnosis_confirm_type records how each label was reached, using one of five methods: histopathology, a single contributor's clinical assessment, serial imaging showing no change, single-image expert consensus, or confocal microscopy with consensus dermoscopy. This allows labels to be weighted or stratified by reliability. For melanomas, mel_thick_mm (Breslow thickness), mel_mitotic_index (categories per mm²) and mel_ulcer (ulceration) support models that predict prognostic features rather than only a diagnosis, in line with the dermatoscopy-based metastasis-prediction work described in Section 1 [37].

Searching by image

The Archive now also offers content-based image retrieval (CBIR), built on the attribute-grounded model of Torop et al. [29] described in Section 1. Instead of filtering by metadata, a user starts from an image and retrieves visually similar images from the Archive. The underlying model can also specialize the search to a quantitative attribute such as lesion area, so that results match the query both in appearance and in that measurement. This makes it practical to assemble look-alike sets for reader studies and teaching, to find hard negatives and near-duplicates when building training and test splits, and to compare a new contributor's images with what the Archive already holds. Like the metadata fields above, it is a capability that few users yet know about.

Using these fields well

The ISIC Archive currently supports only the structured data fields described in the data dictionary. Contributors who want to share data beyond these fields can still do so through DOI sidecar files; however, information in those extra fields can be accessed only through the collection, not through the gallery's faceted search or the API. The opportunity runs in both directions: researchers can use far more of the Archive than they currently do, and contributors can make their collections more useful by filling in these fields.

Who funds the work

The grants behind the Archive and the science around it.

The Archive's infrastructure is funded by two NIH/NCI U24 grants to MSKCC, U24CA264369 (Multimodal-ISIC platform, principal investigator Rotemberg) and U24CA285296 (ISIC-REPO, FAIR compatibility of the Archive, led by Halpern), supported by the MSKCC Cancer Center Support Grant P30CA008748, and by Shore Family philanthropic funding. Who works with whom

Co-authorship among 45 researchers, 2023–2026.

Method in brief

We collected the complete 2023–2026 publication lists of 45 researchers from Google Scholar, Scopus and ORCID, normalized the titles, and linked two people whenever a paper appeared on both lists or a verified author list named both. Restricting to papers on AI, imaging or digital health gave 278 papers with two or more network members. Appendix A describes the method and its limits.

The individual network

The network has four hubs. Queensland is the densest, held together by the ACEMID program: Soyer shares 44 papers with Janda, 30 with Betz-Stablein, 26 with Primiero and 25 with Mar. Barcelona is the next largest; Malvehy and Puig share 67 AI and imaging papers and act as one unit. Vienna (Kittler and Tschandl, 30 shared papers) and MSKCC (Halpern and Rotemberg, 23) complete the core. By weighted degree the most connected researchers are Soyer, Malvehy, Kittler, Rotemberg, Tschandl and Halpern.

The links between hubs run through a small number of people. Kittler shares 18 papers with Malvehy and 16 with Soyer; Soyer shares 17 with Malvehy. MSKCC has fewer joint papers with each of the other hubs than they have with each other. Its central place comes from the Archive, challenges and consensus papers, not from joint clinical studies. The strongest cross-institution link in the United States is Rotemberg–Daneshjou (16 papers), and Daneshjou's connection to the rest of the network runs almost entirely through it.

Within MSKCC, Kose is strongly tied to all three internal groups: the informatics team (Rotemberg 13, Weber 11, Kurtansky 9), the optics group (Rajadhyaksha 10) and clinical dermoscopy (Halpern 9, Marghoob 4). He is also one of ISIC's strong links to an external machine-learning lab, Jennifer Dy's group at Northeastern.

Eleven profiled researchers have no tie of three or more shared papers. For some, this follows from their role (Gutman and Helba are infrastructure contributors; Curiel and Hartman connect through governance). For others it marks an opportunity: Yap, Jaworek-Korjakowska, Han, Tkaczyk, Pacheco, Nicholas and Nelson each run active programs on robustness, validation, data standards or image quality that the core does not yet use.

The institutional network

Aggregated by institution, MSKCC appears on 104 papers, Hospital Clínic Barcelona on 91, Queensland on 85, Vienna on 50 and Monash on 42. The heaviest links are Monash–Queensland (33 joint papers), MSKCC–Vienna (24), MSKCC–Barcelona (21) and Barcelona–Vienna (21). Canfield Scientific is linked to MSKCC, Barcelona, Queensland and Girona. Another big contributor is Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, whose prominence rests on one researcher, Cristian Navarrete-Dechent, a former MSKCC fellow with an exceptionally large dermoscopy output.

The regional network

Across regions, North America appears on 120 papers, Southern Europe on 104, Australia on 102 and Central Europe on 64. The strongest inter-regional links are North America–Southern Europe (36 papers), North America–Central Europe (32), Central Europe–Southern Europe (28) and North America–Australia (26). The United Kingdom and East Asia are almost absent from the co-authorship record despite having AI Working Group members, and Latin America's apparent strength rests on a single researcher. Africa, South Asia and the Middle East do not appear at all, although the Basel group's PASSION dataset from sub-Saharan Africa [93] and MSKCC's RCM work in India [55] show that partners exist.

How the collaboration network was built

Publication lists were collected for the 45 profiled researchers (40 Google Scholar profiles, four Scopus author records and one ORCID record); one further researcher (Maul) was added from a PubMed search, so the individual network can show up to 46 people. Titles from 2023–2026 were normalized and cross-indexed, and two people were linked whenever a paper appeared on both of their lists or a verified author list named both. Prefaces, corrections and replies were excluded, and only papers whose titles concern AI, imaging or digital health were kept (278 papers). Institutions and regions were aggregated so that each paper counts once per institution, region or pair.

The network records co-authorship, not shared data, grants or informal collaboration. Conference abstracts are counted, so pairs that publish an abstract and then a paper are slightly inflated; Google Scholar truncates long author lists, so authorship position is not used; and the topic filter is keyword-based and approximate. Affiliations follow each researcher's profile.

Upcoming grant proposals and collaborations

Three projects now being prepared, with calls and partners.

Evidence-grounded vision-language AI for interpretable skin cancer diagnosis

Call: NIH R01 // Partners: MSKCC, Northeastern, Mayo Clinic

Dermatology lacks a structured, public infrastructure for morphology-grounded AI. Current archives and ontologies like D3X lack localized dermoscopic annotations linked to clinical vernacular and diagnostic reasoning. We propose building an evidence-weighted annotation layer within the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) platform to train, audit, and evaluate an explainable vision-language model (DermVLM²). We hypothesize that anchoring diagnostic predictions to inspectable, localized morphology makes AI safer and more clinically actionable.

  • Aim 1: Construct a Morphologic Knowledge Schema (MKS) and release ~10,000 expert-adjudicated, spatially localized annotations via ISIC.
  • Aim 2: Train DermVLM² to jointly predict diagnoses and localized morphology, audit reasoning via a Logic-Alignment Score, and generate ~250,000 auto-labeled images.
  • Aim 3: Prospectively test whether morphology-grounded explanations improve clinician confidence calibration, management decisions, and resistance to automation bias over standard AI.

Multimodal spatial-temporal AI for lesion-level melanoma triage

Call: Model-to-Clinic (M2C) for Precision Medicine with AI: Integrating Imaging with Multimodal Data (PRIMED-AI) (UG3/UH3, Clinical Trial Optional) // Partners: MSKCC, Stanford University.

Longitudinal melanoma surveillance in high-risk patients requires manually screening hundreds of nevi using 3D total-body photography (TBP) and serial dermoscopy. Current deep learning approaches evaluate cropped lesions in isolation, ignoring patient-level phenotype, spatial context (the "ugly duckling" sign), and temporal change. Consequently, these models suffer from poor calibration and high false-positive rates that limit clinical utility. We propose the Context-Aware Lesion Triage Clinical Decision Support (CDS) framework, a multimodal spatial-temporal AI system designed to align with clinical reasoning. In the UG3 phase, we will:

  • Aim 1: Build a unified multimodal pipeline harmonizing TBP crops, dermoscopy, and clinical covariates for standardized data ingestion and inference.
  • Aim 2: Develop a spatially grounded triage model using patient-specific lesion graphs and graph attention networks to operationalize the "ugly duckling" principle.
  • Aim 3: Construct longitudinal alignment pipelines and temporal embeddings to track individual lesion evolution and phenotypic drift across serial visits.

In the subsequent UH3 phase, we will integrate the validated system into clinical enterprise imaging software (e.g., Canfield Vectra via API), execute prospective clinical trials, and partner with the PRIMED-AI Validation Center for independent evaluation, delivering an interpretable, scalable surveillance tool.

Engagement Platform

Developing robust dermatologic vision-language models requires fine-grained, spatially localized annotations that are expensive and slow to produce by hand. The Engagement Platform extracts these labels directly from expert case reviews by synchronizing interactive annotation tools, real-time mouse tracking, and speech transcription against baseline foundation model proposals.

Prior to each review, the platform populates candidate diagnoses and lesion-level morphologic boundaries using pre-trained dermatology models. As an expert inspects the image, the software aligns the clinician's spoken dialogue with high-resolution cursor movements. This spatial-audio alignment resolves spatial references (such as pointing while naming an atypical pigment network or blue-white veil) and automatically confirms or refutes the model's proposals. The clinician can add direct manual annotations, while an automated check flags any unaddressed candidate findings for brief sign-off before finalizing the case.

The resulting adjudicated cases and spatial interaction logs serve a dual purpose within an adaptive learning environment for trainees. The platform monitors resident cursor navigation, diagnostic choices, and misclassification patterns, using these metrics to detect specific diagnostic blind spots and dynamically serve follow-up cases targeting those errors. Integrated with the International Skin Imaging Collaboration archive, the platform turns routine expert case reviews into a stream of spatially grounded annotations while systematically personalizing clinical instruction for novices.

Researcher profiles

The recent direction of each researcher, grouped by hub.

The profiles below summarize each person's recent direction. They are grouped by hub.

Memorial Sloan Kettering

  • Veronica Rotemberg
  • Allan Halpern
  • Kivanc Kose
  • Jennifer Dy
  • Nicholas Kurtansky
  • Jochen Weber
  • Milind Rajadhyaksha
  • Ashfaq Marghoob

Veronica Rotemberg leads the AI Working Group and the Archive's NIH grants. Her recent work spans 3D-TBP triage, prospective validation, skin-tone measurement, consumer apps and LLM use, consent and privacy, and increasingly policy: journal AI guidelines [94], AI in residency training [95], the environmental cost of AI [96], and a 2026 editorial on AI screening and overdiagnosis [78]. Allan Halpern, ISIC's founder, co-authors most of MSKCC's imaging work, including 3D phenotype studies, longitudinal dermoscopy and crowdsourced annotation, and co-edits the ISIC workshop proceedings.

Kivanc Kose is the group's broadest technical contributor, with 35 papers in 2023–2026. He was joint senior author of the ISIC 2024 triage analysis [2] and built the SLICE-3D duplicate-detection pipeline with Jochen Weber [1]. He leads RCM-AI work in melanoma, basal cell carcinoma and oral cancer [52–54], wrote the field's commentary on federated learning with Rotemberg [97], is senior author of the group's first multimodal-LLM study [29], and co-authored the calibration and eye-tracking papers [8, 33]. Through Jennifer Dy's group at Northeastern he connects ISIC to machine-learning theory (SmoothHess) [98] and generative methods for confocal imaging [56]. Nicholas Kurtansky is the Archive's dataset architect and lead analyst for SLICE-3D and ISIC 2024. Jochen Weber runs Archive informatics, annotation tooling and data quality control. Milind Rajadhyaksha leads confocal instrumentation, including a portable confocal ophthalmoscope and the oral-cancer initiative in India. Ashfaq Marghoob anchors dermoscopy consensus and education and senior-authored the eye-tracking study.

Vienna

  • Harald Kittler
  • Philipp Tschandl

Harald Kittler is the most frequent senior author across hubs, linking Vienna with Queensland, Barcelona, Monash and MSKCC. His recent work includes MILK10k, BALD and DERMA-OCTA [28, 40, 79], the reinforcement-learning paper [32], the "reality check" review [6], commentaries on AI scoring standards and foundation models [99, 100], and the metastasis-prediction reader study [37]. Philipp Tschandl leads dataset and benchmark building (MILK10k, MIDAS, Cleanpatrick) [28, 39, 45] and human–AI studies, including the Nature Medicine 2026 explainability study [36] and the LLM false-reliance work [63]; his single-author review "Developments in digital intelligence for dermatology" [101] shares almost the title of this talk.

H. Peter Soyer has the largest output in the network (184 items in 2023–2026) and led the 3D-TBP randomized trial [4]. Monika Janda leads the behavioral, consumer-app and screening-policy work and the MEL-SELF trial. Brigid Betz-Stablein is the core of Queensland's 3D-TBP analytics. Clare Primiero is an under-recognized connector: co-first author of the 2026 careers consensus [102], first author of the iToBoS annotation protocol [19], and a PanDerm author [3], linking Queensland with Barcelona, Monash and the US. Liam Caffery leads the Metadata and DICOM Working Group and Australian teledermatology and LLM policy [66]. Victoria Mar at Monash leads the ACEMID cohort; Zongyuan Ge's Monash lab builds PanDerm, MAKE, DermAgent and related models, and co-authored the paper on their limits. Pascale Guitera in Sydney bridges 3D-TBP triage and RCM, and leads AI-in-general-practice feasibility work ("One million skin checks") [103] and the UK DermDx triage study [104].

Barcelona and Girona

  • Susana Puig
  • Rafael Garcia

Josep Malvehy and Susana Puig lead a program that is larger than earlier searches suggested. It now centers on LC-OCT (including multicenter AI-assisted diagnosis), autonomous total-body and non-contact dermoscopy devices, real-world evaluation of AI tools in high-risk patients, explainable AI, and prognosis from multi-omic data. Puig coordinates MELCAYA. Rafael Garcia's Girona lab, mostly an underwater-robotics group, continues the iToBoS scanner engineering. Marc Combalia, now in industry, continues to publish on multimodal prognosis with the Barcelona group.
